abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive zero/few-shot inference and generation quality for high-resource languages (HRLs). A few of them have been trained on low-resource languages (LRLs) and give decent performance. Owing to the prohibitive costs of training LLMs, they are usually used as a network service, with the client charged by the count of input and output tokens. The number of tokens strongly depends on the script and language, as well as the LLM’s subword vocabulary. We show that LRLs are at a pricing disadvantage, because the wellknown LLMs produce more tokens for LRLs than HRLs. This is because most currently popular LLMs are optimized for HRL vocabularies. Our objective is to level the playing field: reduce the cost of processing LRLs in contemporary LLMs while ensuring that predictive and generative qualities are not compromised. As means to reduce the number of tokens processed by the LLM, we consider code-mixing, translation, and transliteration of LRLs to HRLs. We perform an extensive study using the IndicXTREME classification and six generative tasks dataset, covering 15 Indic and 3 other languages, while using GPT-4 (one of the costliest LLM services released so far<sup>1</sup> ) as a commercial LLM. We observe and analyze interesting patterns involving token count, cost, and quality across a multitude of languages and tasks. We show that choosing the best policy to interact with the LLM can reduce cost by _∼_ 90% while giving better or comparable performance, compared to communicating with the LLM in the original LRL.

bibliographic.title: Cost-Performance Optimization for Processing Low-Resource Language Tasks Using Commercial LLMs

content.problem: Commercial LLM APIs charge by token count, and low-resource language inputs get over-segmented into many subword tokens because popular LLM vocabularies favor high-resource languages, making LRL usage disproportionately expensive.
content.proposed_solution: The authors preprocess LRL client messages before sending them to GPT-4 using translation to English (open-source MT, explicit GPT-4, implicit GPT-4), word-mixing of heavily fragmented words, and transliteration to Latin script, and introduce the RTPCR metric to rank these policies by performance gained per unit of token-driven cost.
content.algorithm_or_model: RTPCR (RelaTive Performance to Cost Ratio) with translation, wordmix, and transliteration preprocessing of GPT-4 inputs
dataset_testbed: IndicXTREME classification tasks (IndicSentiment, IndicXParaphrase, IndicCOPA, IndicXNLI, Alexa Intent Classification)
GPT-4 (GPT-4-0613) API on a 16GB RAM CPU system, covering 15 Indian languages plus Thai, Swahili, and Chinese

metrics.name: RTPCR
metrics.condition: Translation via IndicTrans, averaged across languages on IndicSentiment classification, relative to native script

metrics.name: RTPCR
metrics.condition: Translation via IndicTrans, averaged across languages on the Samanantar machine translation task

metrics.name: Change in token generation per instance
metrics.condition: Translation via IndicTrans versus native script, averaged across languages on IndicSentiment

metrics.name: Change in token generation per instance
metrics.condition: Translation via IndicTrans versus native script, averaged across languages on XLSUM summarization

metrics.name: Change in accuracy
metrics.condition: Translation via IndicTrans versus native script, averaged across languages on IndicSentiment

metrics.name: Cost reduction
metrics.condition: Approximate maximum reduction when using the best policy (free open-source MT translation) compared with communicating in the original LRL

content.claim: Choosing the best preprocessing policy, chiefly free open-source MT translation to English, cuts GPT-4 API cost by up to about 90% while giving better or comparable task performance relative to using the original LRL text.
author_stated_limitations: They experiment with only one commercial LLM, GPT-4, because of cost constraints, although adding other paid LLMs would make the observations more robust.
The wordmix technique replaces LRL words with translations without considering sentence context, which is crude and sometimes damages sentence structure.
The study is restricted to Indian languages, covering 15 of them, and does not test low-resource languages from other regions.

evidence.problem_quote: If the client’s language is a LRL, chances are, the LLM will heavily segment the LRL tokens into subwords, because LRL subwords have minority status in most popular LLMs today (Hong et al., 2021). Consequently, use of the LLM will be expensive compared to HRL clients.
evidence.proposed_solution_quote: The tool at our disposal is to preprocess the LRL messages from client to LLM service, in the face of a black-box service that we cannot influence. Specifically, we try to decrease the API cost by reducing the number of tokens exchanged between the client and LLM, while trying to maintain task quality.
evidence.claim_quote: We show that choosing the best policy to interact with the LLM can reduce cost by ∼ 90% while giving better or comparable performance, compared to communicating with the LLM in the original LRL.
author_stated_limitation_quotes: For this reason, and to contain costs, we only experiment with one commercial LLM, GPT-4. Although it will increase the experiment cost significantly, bringing other paid LLMs into the experimental setup will make our observations more robust.
Also, our wordmix technique, where we replace an LRL word with its translation, without taking sentence context into account, is crude — it sometimes impacts sentence structure.
In this work, we only focus on Indian languages. Although we cover as many as 15 languages, an immediate extension can be to check the hypothesis for other LRLs worldwide.
